phase1.intro:
Every program you've built so far has quietly assumed things go right. Reality doesn't cooperate that reliably.

Where should we start?

dialogue: [[key:An exception is Java's way of interrupting normal execution the moment something goes wrong]], instead of letting your program silently do the wrong thing or crash somewhere unrelated later.

Picture driving: normal flow is smooth driving. A flat tire is an exception — annoying, recoverable. The engine catching fire is closer to an [[term:Error]] — something so serious the trip's over, no fixing it mid-drive.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚨 an interruption the moment something goes wrong
stickyNote.definition: An exception interrupts normal execution when something goes wrong, rather than letting the program silently misbehave or crash unrelated code later.

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
dialogue: Every exception is a Throwable underneath. [[term:Error]] covers genuinely serious problems (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) your code almost never recovers from. [[term:Exception]] is the family you work with day to day.

[[term:Checked exceptions]] (IOException, SQLException) are things the compiler forces you to acknowledge, with try-catch or throws. [[term:Unchecked exceptions]] (RuntimeException and below — NullPointerException, ArithmeticException) are optional to handle, and almost always signs of an actual bug.

stickyNote.flavor: ✅ compiler-enforced vs. optional but usually a bug
stickyNote.definition: Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) must be handled or declared. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException family) are optional and usually indicate a bug.

topics.buttonText: What am I actually looking at in a stack trace?
dialogue: [[warn:When an exception isn't caught anywhere, Java prints a stack trace and the program crashes]] — and that stack trace is genuinely useful, not just scary red text.
[[key:The first line names the exception, and the line right under it points at the exact file and line number where it happened]] — that's almost always where to start looking.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔍 first line names it, next line points at it
stickyNote.definition: A stack trace printed on an uncaught exception names the exception on the first line and the exact file/line it occurred on the next — start there.

phase1.openingDialogue: An exception interrupts normal execution the moment something goes wrong — some checked by the compiler, some not, all traceable in the stack trace. 🚨

phase2.explanation:
No broken code this time — just one misconception worth clearing up early.

It's tempting to think "all exceptions must be caught," but [[key:that's only true for CHECKED exceptions]]. Unchecked exceptions — anything under RuntimeException — are legal to leave uncaught; Java just won't stop you from ignoring them, even though ignoring them usually means your program crashes the moment one happens.

FileNotFoundException is checked — the compiler makes you deal with it. NullPointerException is unchecked — the compiler lets it slide, but [[warn:letting it slide doesn't mean it won't happen]]; it just means Java trusts you to have written code that avoids it in the first place. A good rule of thumb: [[key:handle whatever can realistically happen, whether or not Java forces you to]].
phase2.openingDialogue: One habit worth correcting before we go further~

phase3.openingDialogue: Quick check! What do you know about exceptions? 🤔

mcq.question:
Which statement about exceptions is TRUE?

A) NullPointerException is a checked exception
B) All exceptions must be caught with try-catch
C) RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked exceptions
D) Errors can be caught and recovered from
E) Stack traces only show the line where the exception occurred

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia:
[[fun:Fun fact]]: Java's checked-exception system doesn't actually exist in most other mainstream languages — C#, Python, JavaScript, and even Kotlin (which runs on the same JVM) skip it entirely and treat every exception as effectively unchecked. It's one of the more debated design choices in Java's whole history, and you'll get to form your own opinion on it once you've written both kinds yourself.

Since you're diving into unexpected outcomes today: this is a good moment to mention that if anything here is ever genuinely stressful rather than just tricky, it's always fine to step away and come back.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
